title: The court case duration model: the whole pipeline in one notebook
intro_html:
IDSE (CS3006) end-to-end data-science project. This notebook takes real Indian district-court records from the raw download all the way to the model that is live at otlr.vercel.app/model, and explains, at every step, what was done, why, and what came out.

The purpose. Indian district courts are known for delay. We ask: which court cases get stuck, where, and can you tell on the day a case is filed? The answer is useful for planning, not for predicting one person's case: a court registry can estimate how many new filings will still be open in a year, and legal-aid offices can see which kinds of case to steer towards mediation.

The short answer. You can tell what kind of case will be quick. Among real disputes, filing-day information barely predicts which ones finish fast, and almost all of a dispute's time is spent after its first hearing.

It has two parts:

  • Part A, the data analysis pipeline: the question, the data, the mess in it, how it was cleaned, two facts about the data that decide everything else, how the target was labelled honestly, and what the cleaned data shows, and where the time in a case goes.
  • Part B, the machine-learning pipeline: the inputs, the time split, the baselines, the three model families, the model we serve and why, how it was tested on cases it never saw, what drives it, two side analyses (regression on days, k-means on districts), survival curves, its limitations, and one case scored live.

Every number is computed here from the cleaned data on disk (data/clean/10/, produced by scripts/build_dataset.py and scripts/label_cases.py) or read from the reports the scripts wrote (reports/*.json). Nothing is typed in by hand. Where a number is both computed here and in a report, the two are compared and the result is printed. Slow steps (the random forests, the permutation importance) are not redone; their results are read from the reports. All code is the project's own tareekh package (src/tareekh/), not a re-implementation.

Data: Development Data Lab's judicial data (eCourts, filings 2010–2018), licence ODbL v1.0.

stages.title: The question
stages.intro_html:
Why this question. Court delay is a planning problem: registries must staff courts for cases that last years, and legal-aid offices must decide which cases to steer towards settlement. Both need to know which kinds of case get stuck and where, as early as possible.

What. So the model answers one measurable question:

Given only what is known on the day a case is filed in a Tamil Nadu district court, how likely is it to be disposed of within one year?

"Disposed of" means the case ended in that court: a judgment, a dismissal, a settlement, a Lok Adalat disposal, or a file closed because the accused absconded. A transfer to another court is not an end; the case is still going somewhere else.

Why a yes/no question and not "how many days". Many cases in the data had not finished when the data was collected, so their number of days is unknown. A yes/no question with a fixed horizon can be answered honestly for every case that was watched for at least a year (Part A7 shows how).

stages.title: The data and where it came from
stages.intro_html:
What. Development Data Lab (DDL) scraped the government's eCourts portal, removed names, and published one row per case for every district court in India, filings 2010–2018. The download is a Dropbox folder of CSV files inside tar archives: one case file per filing year (16 GB of CSV in total), one file with the law and section of every case, and small "key" files that translate the numeric codes (case type, hearing purpose, disposition) into words.

How we got it. Dropbox only allows downloading the whole folder as one stream, so scripts/fetch_ddl.py reads that stream, keeps only the files we asked for, checks each one against its CRC-32 checksum and stops early. scripts/build_dataset.py then converts the CSVs to parquet (a compact column format) reading every column as text, because codes such as "01" lose their leading zero as numbers and then no longer match the key files.

Licence. The licence file inside the download is ODbL v1.0 (the website says CC BY-NC-SA); ODbL allows this use with attribution.

stages.title: The raw mess, before cleaning
stages.intro_html:
What. Before fixing anything we measured what is wrong. Five problems, each shown with real values from the data:

  1. Missing values hide as blanks and as sentinel codes. A sentinel is a special value that stands for "unknown": here -9998 means "unclear" and -9999 means "missing".
  2. Impossible dates: decisions in the year 0001 or 7201, 5000-01-01 placeholders, and cases "decided" before they were filed.
  3. One law, thousands of spellings. Law names are typed by court staff: 29,857 distinct strings for what are a few dozen laws.
  4. Court names are free text with typos ("trail", "musif", "subardinate").
  5. Section numbers are free text too: "138r/w142", "OVIIR1".

Why measure first. Every cleaning rule costs something (a wrong merge is worse than an honest "unknown"), so each rule below reports how many rows it touched.

stages.title: Cleaning, with before and after counts
stages.intro_html:
What. Each problem gets one small, tested function in src/tareekh/ (138 tests, run with uv run pytest):

  • Law names → acts.canonical_act: lower-case, keep letters only, then ordered regular expressions from specific to general; unmatched names stay "Other" rather than being guessed.
  • Section strings → sections.primary_section: keep the first section number and its letter suffix: "304(B)" → 304B, "138r/w142" → 138, "OVIIR1" → Order 7.
  • Court names → courts.court_level: 15 court levels by ordered regular expressions ("Other / unclear" when nothing matches).
  • Dates → cases.decode: parse; anything outside 1950–2022 is blanked and counted; "decided before filing" is flagged.
  • Sentinels → cases.decode: -9998 → "unclear", -9999 → "missing".
  • 52 disposition categories → outcomes.outcome_group: each put in one group: decided, settled, dismissed, disposed, dormant, moved (transfer, committal, remand, referral: the case left, it did not end), interim (bail orders), missing.

Why these choices. We never "repair" a date (we cannot know the intended one) and never guess a law; we count what we could not fix. A moved case is deliberately not treated as finished: treating transfers as endings would make courts look faster than they are.

The cell below applies the real functions and prints how much each one changed.

from tareekh.acts import UNKNOWN, canonical_act
from tareekh.courts import court_level
from tareekh.outcomes import outcome_group
from tareekh.sections import primary_section

named = ~acts_key["law"].isin([UNKNOWN, "Other"])
rows = acts_key["count"].sum()
def share(m):
    return acts_key.loc[m, "count"].sum() / rows

check("share of law rows mapped to a named law", law_named, tn["cleaning"]["law_rows_named"])

    law: {"raw strings": raw_sec[acts.law == law].nunique(),

stages.title: When was the data collected? Estimating the scrape date
stages.intro_html:
What. The data has no "collected on" column, yet that date decides everything: a case with no decision is only known to be still open up to that day. The data leaves a fingerprint: the number of decisions recorded per month runs steadily, then collapses when scraping happened.

How. cutoff.cliff finds the first lasting collapse: the first month that, with the two months after it, sits below a share of the median of the previous twelve months. We use the share 0.5 ("at least half a normal month"), because the scrape ran during February 2019 and a partly scraped month would otherwise make decided cases look pending. It is computed per district, with the state's value as a fallback when a small district's own dip is not a scrape.

Why not "the last normal-looking month". A first version did that and placed Tamil Nadu's cutoff in July 2020: after a scrape the small trickle of re-scraped courts becomes the new normal, so "last normal month" drifts years late. The bug became a test.

from tareekh.cutoff import cliff, cutoffs, with_fallback

monthly = pd.Series(nat["monthly_decisions"])
monthly.index = pd.PeriodIndex(monthly.index, freq="M").to_timestamp()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.8))
ax.plot(monthly.index, monthly.values / 1e3, color=ps.SERIES[0])
normal = monthly.loc["2018"].median()
ax.axvline(pd.Timestamp("2019-02-01"), color=ps.INK_2, lw=1, ls="--")
ax.annotate("collapse: Feb 2019", (pd.Timestamp("2019-03-10"), normal / 1e3 * 0.95), fontsize=9,
            color=ps.INK_2)

      f"February: {monthly.loc['2019-02'].iloc[0]:,.0f}; March: {monthly.loc['2019-03'].iloc[0]:,.0f}.")

stages.title: Labelling "finished within a year" without guessing
stages.intro_html:
What. target.label gives every case two numbers: observed_days, how long we watched it (until it ended, until it moved to another court, or until its district's cutoff), and ended, whether it finished in this court by the cutoff. A case still open at the cutoff is censored: we know it lasted at least that long, not how long in total.

target.within(…, 365) then answers "disposed of within 365 days?" with 1 (ended by day 365), 0 (still open after day 365) or unknown. It is only defined for cases filed at least a year before their cutoff, so that every labelled case had the full year to finish. A case that moved to another court before day 365 stays unknown.

Why the eligibility rule. A first version labelled every case it could. For 2018 filings that meant: cases that finished fast were labelled 1, while their slow neighbours (filed a few months before the cutoff, still open) could not be labelled at all. 2018 came out more than 90% "within a year", which is nonsense. The cell reproduces that trap and then the honest label.

stages.title: Where the time goes in a real dispute
stages.intro_html:
What. Sections A1–A8 show how long cases take. This asks why, as far as the data allows, for real disputes: every case except petty summary trials and bail-type petitions, which are usually over in days. Each case is split at its first hearing:

  • Waiting for the first hearing: filing date to first hearing date.
  • After the first hearing: first hearing to the end of the case, by Kaplan–Meier so that cases still running count instead of being dropped.

Two more views: the gap between a case's latest hearing and its next listed date, and the stage recorded at the latest hearing for cases that were still open when the data was collected.

Why it can't be a model input. Hearing dates happen after filing, so using them to predict from filing day would be leakage. They are used here only to describe what happens.

Data quality. Audited first (filings 2015–2017): 4.7% of first-hearing dates are blank and 0.3% are before filing (both excluded here); the latest hearing date equals the decision date in 80% of finished cases. Each case records only one gap between hearings, so the hearing count below is a rough estimate.

stages.title: The inputs: only what is known on filing day
stages.intro_html:
What. features.build and features.add_law turn each case into 12 inputs, in two sets:

Filing basics

  • district, court_level, case_type (the court's own type code, e.g. os = original civil suit, cc = calendar case, a criminal trial before a magistrate), filing_month;
  • congestion, measured from earlier cases only: log_pending_at_filing (how many cases were already waiting in that district's courts of that level on the filing day), clearance_last_year (how many they cleared in the previous 365 days, relative to that queue) and log_prev_year_filings (filings of the same type in the district the year before). "log" means we use the logarithm, so 10 → 100 matters as much as 100 → 1,000.

+ law and section (from the acts file: what the case was filed under)

  • law (the cleaned law), law_section (the 40 most common law + section pairs, e.g. "Negotiable Instruments Act s.138" = cheque bounce), ipc_bailable, criminal (criminal or civil), n_ipc_sections.

Deliberately excluded. Hearing dates and hearing purposes (they describe the case's future and would leak the answer), the decision date and disposition (the answer itself), the parties' gender (fairness: a public tool must not score people by gender), and the court number (a visitor cannot know which numbered court will get the case).

Leakage means letting the model see information that would not exist at prediction time; it makes test scores look great and the deployed model useless. The vocabularies (which case types and sections get their own category) are decided on the training years only, for the same reason.

stages.title: Baselines, and how we score a prediction
stages.intro_html:
What. Three simple rules every model has to beat, each fitted on 2015–2016 and scored on 2017:

  1. Overall rate: predict the same share for everyone.
  2. Rate per case type: look up the share for that kind of case.
  3. Rate per case type × district: a lookup table by kind of case and district (what a "college predictor"-style website would do). Small groups are shrunk towards the overall rate.

How predictions are scored (the model gives each case a probability of finishing within a year):

  • Accuracy: call it "yes" when the probability is at least 50%; the share of cases where that call was right.
  • AUC: take one case that did finish within a year and one that did not, at random; AUC is the chance the model gave the first one the higher probability. 0.5 = coin toss, 1.0 = perfect ranking.
  • Brier score: the average of (probability − outcome)², the outcome being 1 or 0. Lower is better; always saying 50% scores 0.25.
  • Log loss: also lower is better, but confident wrong answers (saying 95% when the case dragged on) are punished much harder. The model was chosen by log loss.

stages.title: Three model families, with and without the law inputs
stages.intro_html:
What. scripts/train_within_1y.py trained, for each of the two input sets, three families with a small grid of settings:

  • Random forest: hundreds of decision trees, each grown on a random sample of cases and inputs, voting together. Can learn interactions on its own.

Each was fitted on 2015, scored on 2016, and the best setting of each family was refitted on 2015–2016 and scored on 2017. stages.title: How long cases stay open: Kaplan–Meier curves

What. For Tamil Nadu filings 2015–2018, the share of cases still open after N months, estimated with survival.kaplan_meier. At each day it multiplies together the survival of all earlier days: S(t) = Π (1 − dᵢ/nᵢ), where dᵢ cases ended on day i out of nᵢ still being watched. A pending case is watched until the cutoff and then simply leaves the count; a moved case leaves at its move. Nothing is guessed about what happened after we stopped seeing a case.

stages.title: Limitations, stated honestly
stages.intro_html:
What. scripts/experiments.py probed the served model four ways; the results are read here.

  1. Within one kind of case it ranks poorly. AUC inside a single case type is 0.49–0.62 for rent, domestic-violence, maintenance, execution, marriage and civil-suit cases. The model knows which kinds of case are quick; between two cases of the same kind it can barely tell.
  2. Drift. Courts got faster every year, so a model trained on 2015–16 under-predicts 2017 (mean prediction below the observed share). Weighting 2016 more barely helps.
  3. Other horizons. The same recipe for "within 6 months" and "within 2 years" also beats the per-type baseline, so the finding is not specific to one year.

summary_html:
Part A. 81 million raw eCourts rows, read as text; 29,857 law spellings, free-text courts and sections, impossible dates and sentinel codes cleaned by small tested rules with every change counted. Two facts decided the design: the data was collected in January–February 2019 (estimated from the collapse in monthly decisions, per district), and the early years are missing their quick cases, so only 2015–2017 filings are modelled. "Disposed of within a year" is labelled only for cases that had the full year, which removes a bias that had made 2018 look over 90% "fast".

Part B. Twelve filing-day inputs, no leakage, no gender. Train 2015, choose on 2016, test once on 2017. Three model families against three baselines: the law inputs matter far more than the algorithm. The served logistic regression is right about 8 times in 10 on 549,273 unseen cases (AUC 0.873, Brier 0.138 vs 0.844 / 0.163 for a lookup table) and its probabilities are calibrated. That accuracy is mostly easy cases: on real disputes it is right 74.3% of the time against 72.0% for always guessing the commonest answer (B7), and models trained only on disputes do no better. Filing-day information reveals the kind of case and little more; almost all of a dispute's time comes after its first hearing (A9). Within one kind it ranks poorly; courts drifted faster each year. A regression on days and k-means on districts are reported as what they are: exploratory, and weak.
